claims.text: Rapid quenching after solution treatment produces a homogeneous magnetic HEA microstructure, potentially consisting of a single ordered B2 phase.
The proposed intervention is post-solution aging at 650 °C for 24 hours.
Aging at 650 °C for 24 hours will cause the homogeneous magnetic HEA to decompose or precipitate into refined B2/BCC phases.
The aged microstructure will contain a dense distribution of nanoscale precipitates.
Fine precipitates act as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls.
Increased domain-wall pinning requires a higher applied field to reverse magnetization.
Aging at 650 °C for 24 hours will significantly increase coercive field relative to a matched solution-treated and quenched baseline.
The quenched baseline has minimal precipitate-induced domain-wall pinning.
Annealing temperature influences the length scale and phase constitution of B2/BCC decomposition in this class of HEAs.
The coercivity enhancement should hold only when aging produces fine precipitates without excessive coarsening.
Deviating from the specified aging temperature or duration may cause excessive precipitate coarsening or unwanted phase transformations.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase may depend on alloy composition and processing details.
The hypothesis predicts an approximately 20% or greater coercive-field increase as the criterion for a successful result.
